#920. Cast your vote for BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026

Meet the BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contenders

Voting is now open for the BBC World Service Women's Footballer of the Year 2026.

Fans worldwide can vote from the five-player shortlist of Temwa Chawinga, Ewa Pajor, Alexia Putellas, Alessia Russo and Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw.

The vote closes on Wednesday, 18 November at 09:00 GMT.

For the first time in the award's history, the winner will be announced as part of the BBC's Sports Personality of the Year on Sunday, 13 December as well as on the BBC World Service and the BBC Sport website and app.

Contenders for the award - now in its 12th year - are nominated by coaches, journalists and former professionals. It covers the period September 2025-August 2026.

Cast your vote, and read more on the five contenders.

Sorry, this vote cannot be loaded. In order to vote you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

Listen: Who is your BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026?

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Temwa Chawinga

Chawinga has established herself as one of the world's most prolific forwards.

Her impact on the National Women's Soccer League is clear. Her extraordinary form helped Kansas City Current clinch the NWSL Shield as the league's top team in the regular season.

Chawinga scored 15 goals in the 2025 season as she became the first player to be named NWSL MVP in back-to-back campaigns. She also won the Golden Boot for the second year in a row.

Those performances earned her a contract extension through until 2029.

Chawinga returned to international football with Malawi for the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations.

Alongside her sister Tabitha, she helped Malawi reach the country's first Wafcon final and - in doing so - qualify for the Women's World Cup for the first time.

Chawinga scored against Nigeria, Egypt, Ghana and Algeria at Wafcon, winning the tournament's Golden Boot with five goals.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Ewa Pajor

Pajor is widely regarded as a world-class number nine - and it's clear why.

Instrumental as Barcelona won four trophies last season, Pajor scored their first two goals in a 4-0 Champions League final victory over Lyon.

The goals meant she finished as the competition's top scorer, while the result meant she won the Champions League for the first time after losing in five finals - four with Wolfsburg and one with Barcelona.

Pajor also enjoyed an outstanding second season with Barcelona in Liga F, scoring 16 league goals in her 23 appearances and providing five assists. She was a key player as Barca won the domestic treble.

On the international stage, Pajor captains Poland and is the team's leading goalscorer.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Alexia Putellas

Club: London City Lionesses Position: Midfielder

Putellas showed again this year why she is one of the most influential footballers in the world.

After 14 years with Barcelona, she delivered a spectacular final season with the club - helping them win four major trophies.

Her 14 goal contributions in 11 Champions League appearances helped her childhood club win the competition for the fourth time, and she remained a decisive figure bringing experience and leadership when it mattered most.

Putellas delayed announcing her move to London City Lionesses to avoid creating a distraction, but in July 2026 she completed that transfer, saying the club's "women-only identity and ambition" were important factors.

Internationally, Putellas was instrumental in Spain retaining the Women's Nations League in late 2025, scoring three goals against Sweden in the semi-finals before being named player of the finals as Spain defeated Germany 3â0.

Last month she was awarded a record-equalling third Ballon d'Or.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Alessia Russo

Russo has proven to once again be a trusted and integral attacking force for Arsenal, while remaining a key player for England.

She scored 13 WSL goals last season to finish second in the league's scoring charts, and also added six assists in her 22 appearances. In total, she registered 24 goals and eight assists across all competitions.

Among the highlights of her season was winning the inaugural Women's Champions Cup with Arsenal, beating Corinthians 3- 2 after extra time.

It was the first competitive trophy Arsenal's women's team had lifted at the Emirates, though they finished runners-up to Manchester City in the WSL.

Russo remains a first-choice striker for England and in April scored her 30th senior international goal to move into the top 10 of Lionesses goalscorers.

She was also nominated for the PFA Player of the Year award.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Khadija Shaw

After a fine year, Shaw has positioned herself as one of the world's elite forwards.

The defining striker in Manchester City's Women Super League title-winning campaign, she scored 21 goals in 22 league appearances, won a record third consecutive WSL Golden Boot and was named WSL Player of the Season.

Her goals were central to City ending a 10-year wait for the league title.

They went on to complete the Double, with Shaw scoring the opening goal in their FA Cup final victory over Brighton at Wembley to finish the season with 26 goals in all competitions.

She also reached a major personal milestone in December 2025 when she became the first player in the history of City's professional women's team to score 100 goals.

Amid uncertainty over her future, Shaw announced at City's end-of-season celebrations that she had signed a new four-year contract through to 2030.

#919. Which football club has had most international captains in the same team? | The Knowledge

Plus: more speedy marathons by footballers, headed goals of the season and chairs acting as managers

Mail us with all of your questions and answers

“Which club team has had the most international captains playing together at one time?” asks MH Zahid. “Conversely, which international team has had the most club captains in its starting lineup at one time?”

A quick web search finds a fuss being made in various corners of the internet of Chelsea’s 2009-10 squad because it contained six national team captains in Michael Ballack (Germany), Petr Cech (Czech Republic), Didier Drogba (Côte d’Ivoire), Branislav Ivanovic (Serbia), Mikel John Obi (Nigeria) and John Terry (England). These are, indeed, six people who captained their countries, playing together at one time, but crucially they were not all international captains at that time, which because we like to have our hands bound as tight as possible – no questions please – mean they are disqualified from this particular tournament. Ivanovic, you see, was not named Serbia captain until 2012 and Mikel, who was but a whippersnapper at 22 when the 2009-10 season started, was still seven years from getting his hands on the Nigeria armband.

But if that Chelsea team are not themselves the best answer that Knowledge has come up with, they are at least associated with them, having been knocked out of the Champions League by José Mourinho’s captain-strewn Inter. Inter ended up beating Bayern Munich 2-0 in the final, with a team that included the then full-time captains of Brazil (Lúcio), Romania (Cristian Chivu), Cameroon (Samuel Eto’o) and Macedonia (Goran Pandev), while the captain of Serbia (Dejan Stankovic) came off the bench to replace Chivu in the second half and Pandev was replaced by Sulley Muntari, who while not Ghana’s full-time captain had led the side in their most recent game, a 2-1 defeat at Bosnia and Herzegovina that March.

But that’s not all! Among the unused substitutes was Iván Córdoba, who at this point in his career had lost Colombia’s armband to Mario Yepes but been given it back for their previous game, against Paraguay, in the absence of his fellow centre-back. Also in the team and worthy of note, if not of inclusion in our tally of then captains, were Wesley Sneijder, occasional Netherlands skipper and still their all-time record appearance maker, and Javier Zanetti, who regularly captained Argentina and is No 4 on their list of all-time appearance makers (he would be higher had he not been frozen out by their then manager, Diego Maradona, before the 2010 World Cup), with occasional Kenya captain McDonald Mariga also among the subs.

By our count that’s seven players in one matchday squad who could boast of being their country’s current captain at kick-off, and none of whom captained their club side – that honour went to Zanetti. Our searches have not found another team to match that one, but readers have suggested a couple who came close, in the shape of Tottenham in 2020-21 (who boasted five international captains at the time in Hugo Lloris of France; Serge Aurier of Côte d’Ivoire; South Korea’s Son Heung-min; Gareth Bale of Wales; and England’s own Harry Kane, suggested by John Curry) and Liverpool just last year, when in Conor Bradley, Andy Robertson, Virgil van Dijk, Wataru Endo, Mo Salah and Dominik Szoboszlai they had six – though they never played together while they were all incumbent international captains. Any more for any more?

The fastest former footballer we found in time for last week’s instalment was Alexei Smertin, the former Russia and Chelsea midfielder, who screamed around the Kazan Marathon course in 2020 in just two hours, 48 minutes and 17 seconds. But as Richard Askham emailed to point out, that has since been bettered by Joe Skarz, formerly of Bury, Rotherham and Oxford United, and current manager of Golcar United of the Northern Counties East League Premier Division, who in 2025 finished the Yorkshire Marathon with a chip time of 2hr 47min 33sec.

The next question is what level of football do you need to reach to qualify as a footballer? Because Stig Lindmark tipped us off about the former AIK academy player Andreas Almgren, whose dreams of football glory were derailed by injury in his teens and eventually shifted his focus towards distance running. In New York at the start of this month – while the retired cyclist Tom Dumoulin was putting most former footballers to shame with a time of 2:27:12 – he ran his first ever marathon and only went and won the thing, in 2hr 6min 1sec. With no senior competitive appearances he probably does not count, but it’s a good enough effort to get a mention.

“Has a headed goal ever been awarded goal of the season,” wonders Rupert Sheard. “I can think of a few belters, but awards tend to go to ones kicked in.”

“The closest I could get was Robin van Persie’s flying header at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, for the Netherlands against Spain,” writes Sinan Eccles. “He was pipped to the official goal of the tournament by James Rodríguez’s iconic volley, but did make it to third in that year’s Puskas Award – behind Rodríguez and Stephanie Roche.”

Peter Tomlin writes: “Having researched the goal of the season awards in many countries, the only header I could find that won was Keith Houchen’s fantastic one in the 1986-87 FA Cup Final for Coventry v Tottenham. However, Alisson’s dramatic 95th-minute headed winner v West Brom was voted Liverpool’s goal of the season for the 2020-21 season.”

And Mark Johnson points out that Basile Boli’s ridiculous bullet header for Marseille against PSG at the end of the 1993 season would surely have won the Ligue 1 goal of the season award but for the inconvenient fact that no such award existed at the time.

Martyn Amos has responded to last week’s scepticism about the possibility of an Ipswich fan website existing in 1990, the year before the first known website went online. “Just to clarify, the original page was set up by Phil Clarke, who was working at BT Labs in Martlesham (near Ipswich), in 1990,” he writes. “At the time, as I said, the web was still experimental, and I think the page was only available internally. Your correspondent is correct in saying that the first public website appeared in August 1991. But the ITFC page still existed, in some recognisable form, using the standard web technology, in 1990, so I think it counts. That’s my understanding, anyway.”

With Lee Power taking charge of Swindon Town, in last week’s Knowledge archive we dug up our piece from 2006 on chairs acting as managers, we wrote in October 2015. Neil Bellis, the director of communications at Chester FC, writes to point out we missed Terry Smith off our list.

“He took over four games into the season despite not really knowing much about ‘soccer’,” writes Neil. “He was a former American Football coach but for some reason ending up buying our club. Not only did we end up getting relegated from the Football League for the first time in 1999-2000 we also saw a few very strange ideas from him including having a team talk as the Lord’s prayer and appointing a captain in defence, midfield and attack. Thankfully we are now fan owned so this level of insanity shouldn’t happen again.”

One of Smith’s first games as manager was against Aston Villa in the League Cup, a fixture that prompted a visit from ITV to see what was going on. The result of that visit can be seen here:

“There’s nothing magical about being a coach,’ said Smith not long after his arrival. “It’s like being the general manager of a business, the coaching principles are the same in any sport.” That doesn’t sound too promising but things didn’t really go horribly wrong until the end of November, when Chester began a run of 11 defeats in 12 matches. There’s some footage here of the aftermath of the 5-1 home defeat by Leyton Orient just after Christmas – “I want to thank you guys,” says Smith in the dressing room. “That’s the most pitiful, pitiful effort I’ve ever damn seen.”

Smith stepped down as manager and brought in Ian Atkins in January 2000, then sold the club in October 2001.

“What’s the highest score by a team or in a match where no player scored more than one goal?” writes Paul Gage.

“Manchester United have 20 league titles, won by three managers. Liverpool have 20 league titles won by 10. Which teams have the most and fewest titles won by the most and fewest managers?” asks Will Marquand.

“Djed Spence (shirt No 99) set up Pio Esposito (No 94) in Inter’s 2-0 win over Como at the weekend. Has there ever been a combination for a goal (assist and scorer) with a higher combined shirt number than 193?” writes Joe Strawson.

“Did the Fenerbahce side have more combined Premier League appearances than Liverpool in the teams’ recent Champions League match? If so was this the first instance of a club in Europe playing opposition who had more game appearances in their own league than they had themselves?” ponders Josh Wolff-Martin.

#916. Michael Carrick was just the latest fall guy for Manchester United’s dysfunctional hierarchy | Jamie Jackson

Disastrous decisions and confused appointments have been a constant theme at Old Trafford since Sir Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013

For a window into the alarming dysfunction at Manchester United that Michael Carrick failed to manage and caused his sacking, consider the case of Eddie Howe, initially a favourite to succeed the 45-year-old before Mauricio Pochettino’s emergence as the chosen one.

The former Newcastle manager had been Jason Wilcox’s choice to take over from Carrick. Howe was also the favoured candidate of Dan Ashworth, Wilcox’s predecessor as United’s director of football, to follow Erik ten Hag after the Dutchman’s sacking in October 2024. Except Wilcox disagreed and Sir Jim Ratcliffe went with Wilcox’s man, Ruben Amorim, and that December Ashworth departed only five months after joining.

At that juncture Wilcox was the technical director. Now he is United’s highest-ranking football executive, the powerbroker. He was able, apparently with a straight face, to recommend to Ratcliffe that Howe, nearly two years after he rejected him, should become United’s eighth permanent No 1 in the 13 and a half years since Sir Alex Ferguson retired.

If following this is difficult, making sense of it is near impossible. Should London’s West End need a new farce then look no further than the wacky world of Ratcliffe and the football department he leads, which is also headed up by Omar Berrada, the chief executive, and is proving a disjointed, illogical operation.

Yet if this meant Carrick was dealt a treacherous hand, it is also true that he should have played it better. This, after all, is the job of a football coach: to somehow make wine from water – even if the water is murky, and may need purifying first.

José Mourinho, one of Carrick’s predecessors, from May 2016 to December 2018, showed how – to a degree. Mourinho stated famously that leading United to second place in 2017-18 (with 81 points, 19 behind Manchester City) was one of his finest achievements. This from a serial winner who broke the United-Arsenal duopoly of the Premier League to take Chelsea to consecutive crowns (2004-05 and 2005-06), and made history in Italy by guiding Inter to the treble in 2009-10.

Mourinho’s billing of that second place was down to having to negotiate a similar shambles, overseen by Ed Woodward, the then executive vice-chair.

The Portuguese’s opening campaign ended with the Carabao Cup and Europa League collected despite, like Carrick, having to deal with a hierarchy convinced that it knew better than the man it hired as the football expert.

Here we arrive at a fundamental quality Carrick lacked: an ability to be streetwise when really required. For an example of Mourinho’s nous, rewind to a pre-season tour of America when this correspondent was offered an off-the-record sounding about a player he wanted out of the club but the executive did not.

The manager wanted his message out – that this was a player non grata. Machiavellian or pragmatic? A guess says Carrick would never dream of employing a similar tactic to achieve the best result for the team. But why not? Mourinho wanted a bad egg gone before the dressing room was stunk out and on-field prospects undermined.

Carrick, in his last month, encountered two of his own malevolents: Lisandro Martínez, a de facto captain who dared to criticise Wilcox’s recruitment after the 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madrid; and Bruno Fernandes, Carrick’s official leader, who betrayed his manager by questioning his tactics after the 4-1 humiliation at Como.

Each crossed a line and were emblematic of a chaotic changing room, a major factor in the dismal run of three wins from 15 games this season, including elimination from the Carabao Cup, and the league return of eight points from 10 matches that has United in the relegation zone.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Fernandes, Martínez and a club run like a banana republic are the next man’s problem, just as Mourinho inherited from Louis van Gaal, who was sacked the day after winning the 2016 FA Cup, the faults at boardroom level embodied by Woodward.

Here we see the recurring problem at United: a new gun is hired and is bequeathed a sorry mess that is impossible to clean up because there is no true will to eradicate it. Why? Because the only real reset of culture would be for Ratcliffe, who owns 29.4%, Wilcox, Berrada and the Glazer family, whose ownership since 2005 has left the club about £1.2bn in debt, to accept they are the problem and depart.

Carrick is a good guy whose adoration of United was returned to him by the support, underlined by the reception he got from the Stretford End after the 3-0 humbling by Bournemouth last month. Yet being a decent man and head coach was not enough.

In elite sport the fine margins are often trumpeted as the difference between triumph and failure. Last season, from mid-January, Carrick worked these his way as Manchester City, Arsenal, Liverpool and Chelsea were defeated and United lost only two of his 17 games as interim head coach.

This season, though, the fall-off was startling – and Carrick was found wanting. Who knows what might have occurred if United were the “best-in-class” organisation Ratcliffe insisted they would be under him. As with the muddled thinking regarding Howe, “worst in class” may be a more apt characterisation.

The agonising, overlong process to decide Carrick should be sacked was the latest illustration. On Monday evening the Guardian broke the news that Wilcox and Berrada would recommend to Ratcliffe that Carrick should be removed. Yet days passed during which Carrick still took training and it emerged the deal for Pochettino was being finalised. A proper functioning organisation would have acted more swiftly and with more style.

This is what the next manager has to grapple with. He may succeed. But the odds are stacked against it owing to the deep structural faults that undermine the modern Manchester United.

#913. Jonbon records Shloer Chase hat-trick at Cheltenham

The evergreen Jonbon continued his record of never finishing outside the first two places when seeing off Mighty Bandit to land a third Shloer Chase crown at Cheltenham for Nicky Henderson and JP McManus

Harry Cobden made his first ride on Jonbon in public a successful one as the odds-on favourite landed a third Shloer Chase in gritty fashion at Cheltenham.

Never out of the first two in 29 races, Nicky Henderson's charge is approaching veteran status at the age of 10 and was winning for the 21st time in his stellar career.

His task was made easier with the late withdrawal of Gidleigh Park, but Mighty Bandit kept him honest after the last, with the 1-2 favourite pulling away again towards to line to win by two and a quarter lengths.

Cobden said: "I'm so fortunate to be in this position riding all of these great horses and there's so many in the camp to look forward to, you do have to pinch yourself a little bit.

"I was really looking forward to it and pressure is just something you put on yourself isn't it. There was no point having a sleepless night over a Shloer Chase though as what would I be like in March!"

He went on: "I really enjoyed that. He pinged from fence to fence and loved that ground, he did well.

"I didn't want to ask him too many questions too early today as ultimately he is a 10-year-old now, but he's been round everywhere and doesn't need me telling him what to do.

"It was a lovely starting point for me to ride him in. If it was a Champion Chase with 10 others around going championship pace then it wouldn't be as easy, but it was pretty uncomplicated and straightforward there. I just let him enjoy himself."

The man who made the call to employ Cobden was owner JP McManus who has never made any secret of the esteem he holds the veteran in.

McManus said: "Nicky had him looking great and he was up for it today, he gave a little blow but hardly put a foot wrong and got the job done.

"This horse has stood the test of time and he's been going from four to now rising 11 and to run as many times as he has and still be performing, it's fair play to Nicky as he knows this horse to a tee."

He added: "I don't have to worry about Harry, he knows every horse. He was good on him there."

Henderson was equally as delighted as the new green and gold pilot, stating the intention to follow the tried and tested route to Sandown's Tingle Creek on December 5.

"Some say this isn't his favourite place but that's his third win in this race and it's lovely to see him back," said the Seven Barrows handler.

"He is exactly where we want him to be and we have three weeks until the Tingle Creek and that will be the plan.

"I'm always so proud he has never been out of the first two which is going to be a hard record to maintain, but we've kept it intact today and it's a remarkable record.

"I thought he was more forward this year than last year and this was the perfect race for him. He's had a lovely time and Harry looks like he enjoyed it. There was never any anxiety and I think he always had enough in his pocket.

"He'll never run away from them at his age over two miles and we know we can go further. But for now we'll stick to two miles and then review. I could see him doing two and a half at some stage and maybe after the Clarence House like last year, but we'll see."

Rising weighing-room star Daniel King timed his run to perfection aboard the Tom Cooper-trained D Art D Art in the Mucking Brilliant Paddy Power Novices Chase.

The winning jockey, who landed a famous double at the Galway Festival in the Plate and Hurdle for Willie Mullins and Tony Martin respectively in the summer, delivered aboard the 7-2 shot.

Given time to close on the leaders from a patient position in the five-runner field, King closed on the leaders at the turn into the straight and stayed on well to deny the strong-finishing Intosomethinggood at 100-30 by a neck.

Cooper said: "This is very emotional and if you saw this horse on August 13, 2025 he got an awful bad doing. He bled profusely internally and they did a wonderful job at the vets.

"It was terrible, he was gone, dead. But they brought him back to life and it was amazing. He crashed into a wall and got loose in the box and out of his stable overnight and what he did to himself was horrific.

"We gave him a couple of runs to get over the accident and he's taken well to the fences. He can come back here in March, what for I don't know what, but he's obviously going absolutely the right way.

"He's a different horse this year and he's been a little hot before, but he's so chilled out now and changed his tune completely, he's loving life."

He added: "I was always confident as he jumps for fun and this rider is absolutely top drawer - you're going to hear a lot about this kid!

"He doesn't know how to lose this horse and he will stick his head out, grind and wants to win."

#911. ‘Second ball’ may be a Sunday league mantra but Yates showed its top-flight relevance

Midfielder’s old-school attributes came to the fore during Nottingham Forest’s win against Manchester City

Modern football is more systematised and data-driven than ever but some things never change. Winning the first ball is important but the second ball – the holy grail for Sunday league footballers – is often more so.

Nottingham Forest’s 3-1 win against Manchester City last weekend featured a classic example. Forest led 2-1 inside the last 20 minutes but City, lifted by Rayan Cherki’s sweet half-volley, were pushing for an equaliser.

Another City attack comes down their right: after Jair Cunha’s clearing header from a deep Matheus Nunes cross, the ball loops up in the air before descending inside the home penalty area.

Ryan Yates, Forest’s old-fashioned midfield general, is being pressed from behind by the Argentina international Enzo Fernández as the ball drops. Yates stands his ground, using his strength to hold off his opponent’s muscular challenge. Fernández tries to impose himself, too, but ends up on the turf.

Not only does Yates win that crucial one-on-one, by cleverly improvising an overhead kick to shift the ball away from danger he inadvertently begins a counterattack that arguably changes the course of Forest’s season.

Liam Delap shepherds the ball to Morgan Gibbs-White. Enzo Maresca’s team are hopelessly exposed and Gibbs-White devours the space in front of him with a driving run.

He lays a pass off to Delap, who takes one touch before swerving a sensational shot into the far corner for 3-1. It is a memorable move that will surely compete for goal of the month. But none of it would have been possible without the dirty work of Yates: a show of strength and desire from the captain at the other end of the pitch.

Oliver Glasner understands the importance of the moment and sprints to celebrate with his players. After a barren scoring run Delap suddenly has two goals in one afternoon. The home fans are delirious. Twelve seconds after Yates won the duel, Forest have a two-goal cushion rather than a desperate fight to maintain their lead.

The second ball is a pleasingly old-school term but remains of paramount importance. Visit your local amateur club and you are likely to hear it being shouted as a motivational mantra.

At grassroots level it’s a reminder to teammates that finesse and creativity are all very well, but it’s hard work, desire and a refusal to let your opponent get the better of you that win matches.

And it remains part of the elite game’s lexicon. Premier League managers sometimes point to upcoming opponents’ second-ball prowess – a back-handed compliment if ever there was one. The hidden meaning: “They feed off scraps at set pieces. They don’t create from open play.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

After seeing Southampton Under-21s lose to Wealdstone in the National League Cup a couple of years ago, I mentioned to the then Saints manager, Simon Rusk, that his goalkeeper had been shouting “second ball” throughout.

“To be honest,” Rusk replied with amusing frankness, “I’m not sure some of them even know what second ball means.”

Managers like relying on data. They like predictable outcomes. They prefer to remove risk, reduce chaos and exert control over as much of the game as possible. But while the outcome of a one-on-one duel can never be certain, the consequences can often be far-reaching. That’s why second balls matter.

Against City Yates was named in Forest’s starting lineup, and given the captain’s armband, for the first time this season. Glasner, asked how he had motivated his players, revealed: “Ryan Yates spoke. I played more than 500 games as a player, I’ve managed, I don’t know, 500 games … and I’ve never heard such an inspiring speech.”

Glasner’s captain backed up stirring words with action. If there was a sense Yates’s star was fading – that his attributes of graft, tenacity and box-to-box drive were losing currency – then it was emphatically extinguished at the City Ground.

Win the first one if you can. But it’s the second ball that often makes the difference.

#910. Sarah Paulson Reveals Why She Will Never Marry Holland Taylor

Sarah Paulson, who began dating Holland Taylor in 2015, explained why she has no plans to marry the Two and a Half Men alum: “I’m happy that I haven’t been married.”

All’s fair in Sarah Paulson’s relationship with Holland Taylor—except for marriage.

Despite being together for more than a decade, the All’s Fair actress—who began dating Taylor after reconnecting in 2015—emphasized that tying the knot with the Two and a Half Men alum is off the table.

“I'm happy that I haven't been married,” Paulson said on the Nov. 12 episode of Chelsea Handler’s Dear Chelsea podcast. “I feel that I've maintained some sense of myself in a way.”

But while the 51-year-old—who previously dated Cherry Jones from 2004 to 2009—may not call Taylor her wife, that doesn’t mean their relationship is a horror story.

“The bond, the connectivity I have with Holland, I feel married to her,” Paulson continued, “but I don't have or have never had the need to have it be something written in stone somehow. The stoneness of it gives me the heebie-jeebies.”

Noting the “freedom” that being unmarried provides, the American Horror Story star added, “It’s not about being away from her or being with another person, it's just about maintaining some sense of my own independence.”

“We just have never, ever felt the need to [get married],” Paulson added, adding that she feels “as connected to another person as I possibly could to Holland.”

The longtime couple are also on the same page when it comes to kids.

“I like my life. I'm happy that I haven't had children,” Paulson said. “I know that I don't have the constitution to raise a creature, a person, a being, and then be like, ‘Oh, he'll have a wonderful day outside and I hope it's great.’ I can just see myself following them.”

So, not having kids is a way for the Ratched alum to protect her well-being.

“My heart is too fragile,” she explained. “I feel too many things. It's too much for me.”

She's an introvert, she said, "maybe a step away from being a straight-up loner"; he's the ultimate extrovert "the mayor of everywhere," as he put it. She's a touch messy; he's "a little OCD" noted the Oscar winner. But, wed since 2003, they've long since learned to let the other do their thing. That's the advice the How to Get Away With Murder lead said she gives to all her soon-to-be-wed friends. "Marriage does not start when you walk down the aisle," she shared. "Your marriage starts when you look over at a person who you love more than anything, and there's something about him—just one character trait that makes you say to yourself, 'Oh man, that's going to drive me crazy. I don't know if I can deal with this.' And then the next minute you say, 'But you know what? I love him.' That's when your marriage starts."

You don't reach the 50-year mark in any relationship by letting disagreements drag on. Any time there's a blowup, noted the Grace and Frankie star, "Usually, I'm the one who apologizes. It's not hard because I love her and can't bear for her to feel lonely for even five minutes." Even better is when she can avoid saying she's sorry to the writer altogether. Her top takeaway, she shared, "Remember, when you're angry at your partner and say something hurtful, you will be more angry at yourself later for having said hurtful things to the person you love. You'll feel angry twice. Not good for your blood pressure, and certainly not good for your relationship."

Few things are more on brand than former New York State Supreme Court judge Jerry declaring their decades-long union works because he usually lets the Judge Judy icon win. But for his bride it's more about knowing you're not always going to like the final verdict. Their 12-year marriage dissolved in 1990 when he couldn't be the caretaker she needed following her father's death. Yet, when they got back together one year later and quickly remarried, she had no delusions that he was suddenly going to be the type to run the household or take the lead on birthday plans. "Every relationship is different, but there is a common thread of unhappiness, and that unhappiness comes from trying to make another person different from who they are. You can try, but they're always going to resent it," she explained matter-of-factly. "I don't think you should marry anyone with the expectation of changing who they are."

The Lost alum would be, well, lost without his longtime love, who he married in 1993. As he explained to E! News in April 2025, "My wife—being patient as I traipse around the world, going from job to job—she's kept our family stable. She's been fantastic."

Calling her a "very patient woman," the actor said his wife and their two sons keeps him "humble no matter what's happening."

"They shape my values," he added. "It's great to have that perspective and North Star."

#908. BBC to show Dover v Leicester and Salisbury v Blackpool

Leicester City will travel to Crabble, the home of Dover Athletic of National League South

Non-league clubs Dover Athletic and Salisbury will stage the BBC's two chosen FA Cup second-round ties next month.

National League South side Dover welcome former Premier League and FA Cup winners Leicester City to Crabble on Saturday, 5 December (17:15 GMT, BBC Two/iPlayer).

Another sixth-tier side, Salisbury, will host Blackpool, winners of one of the most memorable finals of all time in 1953, at the Raymond McEnhill Stadium the following day (Sunday 6 December, 12:15 GMT, BBC Two/iPlayer).

Dover reached the second round courtesy of a 2-0 home win over National League side Wealdstone and are seeking to reach round three for just the third time in their history, having lost against Huddersfield in 2011 and at home to Premier League outfit Crystal Palace in 2015.

The Foxes - who lost on their first four FA Cup final appearances before Youri Tielemans' goal secured a 1-0 win over Chelsea in the 2021 final - now play in League One after back-to-back relegations and overcame Oxford City of National League North 4-2 in the first round.

Salisbury are yet to concede a goal in their three ties this season and thrashed Sholing 6-0 to reach round two for the first time since the club was reformed in 2015.

Seventh-tier sides Wimborne Town and Plymouth Parkway will also see their home ties against League One Bradford City and League Two Barnet, respectively, televised among the eight selected for live coverage across the weekend.

All clubs featured in live television broadcasts will receive Â£60,000 while the winning and losing clubs in the second round will receive Â£79,500 and Â£21,200 respectively from the competition prize fund.

The third round draw will take place before the televised tie between Guiseley and Notts County at 19:30 GMT on Monday, 7 December.

A comprehensive highlights programme will cover the weekend's action on Sunday, 6 December at 17:10 GMT (BBC Two/iPlayer).

All of the second round's goals will be available to view across BBC digital platforms including the BBC Sport website and app.

All eight televised cup ties are on TNT/HBO Max with the ties at Dover and Salisbury also on BBC Two/iPlayer.

Crewe Alexandra v Plymouth Argyle (15:15 GMT)

All other fixtures will take place at 15:00 GMT on Saturday, 5 December. Fixtures and kick-off times are subject to change. The BBC is not responsible for any changes that may be made.

#907. Jack Nicholson’s Son Ray Makes Confession About Their Relationship

Jack Nicholson's son Ray Nicholson revealed what his relationship with his father is actually like, admitting that he was "really scared" to tell his father he wanted to act.

Jack Nicholson’s son Ray Nicholson is shining a light on their relationship.

The Smile 2 actor—whom Jack shares with ex Rebecca Broussard—revealed that much of his relationship with his 89-year-old father stemmed from their mutual affection for sports as he noted the two “can’t talk” about many other topics.

“I love sports so much. It’s also the language of love that me and dad share,” Ray shared in a conversation with sister Lorraine Nicholson for Interview Magazine published Nov. 11. “We can’t talk about a lot, but we can talk about the f--king Lakers until kingdom come.”

And while the two had plenty to discuss about Ray’s high school football career, it was more difficult for the 34-year-old to tell his father he wanted to pursue acting, admitting, “I was really scared to tell dad.”

Still, he knew it was the right move for him, especially after an injury and staph infection after his final high school football game made him realize that pursuing football in college wasn’t as good as it gets.

As he recalled, “It was this voice-of-god moment that was like, ‘You don’t want to do this. You want to be an actor.’”

Despite being descended from Hollywood royalty, Ray knew it wouldn’t be an easy ride, although he was certainly aided by what he learned in film school.

“I went to USC and learned to love everything about filmmaking,” he said. “My education really taught me that dad isn’t god. He’s not the only thing in this film industry.”

“He’s a beautiful part of it, but a very small part,” Ray continued. “Yes, of course, making dad proud is high on my list, but this is really a way of finding who I am.”

And for now, the Mosquito Bowl actor certainly felt that he was “on the right path to that.”

But even when Ray was a teenager, Jack always knew his son would follow the path that was best for him.

“Ray might not tell you exactly what he’s up to,” Jack shared with AARP Magazine in 2008, “but once he’s got his mind set on something, he’s gonna stick to it and take care of business, no matter what me or anybody else says.”

As for Jack, the Chinatown star—who in addition to Ray and Lorraine, 36, is dad to kids Jennifer, 62, with ex-wife Sandra Knight, Caleb, 55, with Susan Anspach, Honey, 44, with Winnie Hollman, and Tessa, 32, with Jennine Gourin—has kept a low profile in recent years after retiring from acting.

But as his friend Michael Douglas noted, it’s certainly a right Jack has earned after spending over five decades in Hollywood.

“I still see him, but he is fine. He is up there by his house and walking around in his slippers,” Michael said in October, according to The Independent. “He deserves it. I understand.”

For a look at more stars who have departed Tinseltown, keep reading.

After the Mask of Zorro actor suffered a near-fatal heart attack in 2019, he moved back to his native Málago, Spain, to focus on his love of theater.

“It changed the way I look at life,” Banderas told The Times in March 2026. “Faced with death, it made me look back and realise that I am, in fact, a theater actor.”

Now, the Tony nominee—who still occasionally takes on TV and film projects—owns a theater venue and gets involved with the local community.

“I have never been so happy,” he continued. “It keeps me in touch with my roots, my neighbourhood, my people. I haven’t lost that connection over the years. Quite the opposite.”

Before landing a role in Prime Video's Every Year After, The Girl Next Door actress took a four-year break from acting, leaving L.A. to raise her two kids with husband Dion Phaneuf.

"I realized I worked all four years through our first child and it was really hard," Cuthbert confessed in June 2026 during an appearance on Today, "to separate that mom from the working person I was. So, when we had our second, I just felt like I didn't want to waste any second of it and I didn't want to be on set."

Cuthbert—best known for starring in '00s films like Old School as well as hit TV shows including 24 and Happy Endings—added, "I just felt like I needed to be at home with the kids and I enjoyed every minute."

The actress, known for her roles on hit TV dramas like Fire Country, Numb3rs and Rescue Me, shared in July 2026 that she sold her Los Angeles home after living there for 30 years to embark on her "third chapter" somewhere far away from Hollywood.

"I came here chasing a dream that I am still shocked worked out," she wrote on Instagram. "And I also got to raise babies in the sun and the mountains and enjoy this beautiful home and attend public schools ?? Pinch me I’m overwhelmed by the blessings and hope, really hope I gave enough back. LA will always be where my family is from."

The Ellen DeGeneres Show host's eponymous talk show ended in 2022 after a 19-season run amid allegations of a toxic work environment that prompted an internal investigation, multiple firings of executives and public ire.

DeGeneres returned to the spotlight for her final standup special For Your Approval, which released on Netflix in September 2024. During the lead-up to that special, she revealed she would be leaving Hollywood altogether.

"This is the last time you’re going to see me," she told a crowd during her Ellen’s Last Stand…Up tour, per SFGate. “After my Netflix special, I’m done."

DeGeneres and her wife Portia de Rossi have since moved to the Cotswolds, deciding to stay put in November 2024 after Donald Trump's reelection, the talk show host told to Richard Bacon in a July 2025 conversation at the Everyman theater in Cheltenham.

"It's absolutely beautiful," she gushed about the English countryside, per the BBC. "We're just not used to seeing this kind of beauty. The villages and the towns and the architecture—everything you see is charming and it's just a simpler way of life.

"It's clean," DeGeneres continued. "Everything here is just better—the way animals are treated, people are polite. I just love it here. We moved here in November, which was not the ideal time, but I saw snow for the first time in my life. We love it here. Portia flew her horses here, and I have chickens, and we had sheep for about two weeks."

One of the reasons the America's Next Top Model host moved to Australia? To stay on top of her ice cream brand."So I have this ice cream company, SMiZE and Dream," Banks explained on an April 2025 episode of Today with Jenna & Friends. “But we've been more what we call B2B, like on an airplane and on cruises. I’ve been going to Australia a lot because we were making a lot of our ice cream there in a big facility doing our recipes. And I just fell in love with it every time I went back and went back."Not only was she happy there, but she also knew it was a good market for her business."The three countries that eat the most ice cream?" she continued. "America, New Zealand and Australia."So, the supermodel moved to Australia with her son York (his dad is her ex Erik Asla) and boyfriend Louis Bélanger-Martin, noting, "Australia has been a dream come true for me and my family."

While it's been a minute since the Desperate Housewives star lived on Wisteria Lane, she's since found a new address IRL."I had my whole adult life here," Eva told Marie Claire in November 2024 about leaving Los Angeles. "But even before [the pandemic], it was changing. The vibe was different. And then Covid happened, and it pushed it over the edge. Whether it’s the homelessness or the taxes, not that I want to s--t on California—it just feels like this chapter in my life is done now."So for the past few years, the actress, her husband José Bastón and their son Santiago have split their time between Mexico and Spain."I’m privileged," she continued. "I get to escape and go somewhere. Most Americans aren’t so lucky. They’re going to be stuck in this dystopian country, and my anxiety and sadness is for them."However, Eva noted her move wasn't because of President Trump's re-election."I didn't leave because of the political environment," the Flamin' Hot director said on The View: Behind the Table podcast in November 2024. "I left because my work took me there since Land of Women—shooting six months in Catalonia, then four months in Mexico for Searching for Mexico, then back to Spain. Now I've been there for years. So I just don't like that it's politicized."Since moving, Eva has continued to stay busy, with recent projects including her roles in Only Murders in the Building and Alexander and the Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad Road Trip.

The actor has gone from Chicago to Spain."My wife is Spanish, and she gave me about seven years here," Richard said of Galicia native Alejandra Silva on a November 2024 episode of The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. "And so we're going to spend some years in Madrid."He also expressed his excitement over what the move would give the couple's young sons Alexander and James."Our kids are bilingual," Richard, who also has an adult son Homer with ex Carey Lowell, added, "so they're going to flourish there."Indeed, it seems the whole family has."The truth is that you are seeing us in our momentum," The Agency: Central Intelligence star told Elle España in January 2025. "We are happier than ever."

From AM to PM, the singer is living in Paris "My husband is French, and we've been together for over seven or eight years," Milian, who is married to singer Matt Pokora, said on a November 2024 episode of The Jennifer Hudson Show. "And for the last three or four years we were commuting back and forth every six months."However, they decided to officially say au revoir to the U.S. so her kids—who include daughter Violet from her former marriage with The-Dream and sons Isaiah and Kenna from her union with Pokora—could study in France."They're all going to school in Paris," she continued. "I was like, 'What better than an opportunity than that?"And life for the family appears to be magnifique."My kids are happy there," the Dexter: Original Sin actress told E! in December 2024. "They know French. We go to the park. I have an active lifestyle that's really nice during the day. Then at night time, I do my work because I work hours ahead. It's a nice, healthy balance for me."

The Mean Girls star is tired of rumors starting about why she left Los Angeles.So, she set the record straight while looking back at her hectic work schedule and partying in the aughts. "I feel like some of [my work] got overshadowed by paparazzi and all that kind of stuff when I was younger, and that’s kind of annoying," the Parent Trap alum told Bustle in March 2024. "I wish that part didn’t happen. I feel like that kind of took on a life of its own. So that’s why I wanted to disappear. I was like, 'Unless there’s no story here, they’re not going to focus on just my work.'"Lohan moved abroad—first to London then to Dubai (also opening beach clubs in Greece). However, there was another reason she sought a life away from the spotlight.

"I was like, 'What if I never fall in love? What if this never happens?'" she added. "And it took me just taking time for me for all those doors to open and the ‘yeses’ to come—the things I wanted to say 'yes' to."Of course, Lohan did find love with Bader Shammas, the pair marrying in 2022 and welcoming son Luai the following year. They still live in Dubai, but the Freaky Friday actress hasn't left the Hollywood industry completely, starring in movies like Our Little Secret, Irish Wish and Freakier Friday.

For Hartnett, the decision to leave Hollywood came after some self-reflection."Hollywood is more than a place; it's like a state of mind," the Black Mirror actor told People in July 2024. "If you're around people who are constantly talking about the movie business, your life is going to be pretty much one note. And I've never wanted that."Instead, he wanted more."I've always wanted to be around ... people generally doing lots of other things that would bring my mind off of my work and force me to grow in different directions," Hartnett added. "To me, that's the spice of life."So, the Black Hawk Down alum, his wife Tamsin Egerton and their four kids moved to England's Hampshire countryside."Time passes quickly," he told The Guardian in July 2024. "With four children, you have so much to do. In a way, less is happening. But more of the important stuff is happening."Still, Hartnett has stayed plenty busy and landed roles in Verity, Fight or Flight and Trap.

If you haven't checked your social network lately, then you might not know that Eisenberg doesn't live in L.A."I’ve lived in Indiana for the last decade on-and-off," the A Real Pain star told CBS News Sunday Morning in February 2025. "That’s where I feel the most comfortable. I’m not somebody who wants to surround myself in an industry that just feels kind of unstable to me."And while he's an Oscar nominee, he lives a pretty normal life with his wife Anna Strout and son Banner."I'm not on social media, and I'm not a person who's on the phone with industry people all the time," Eisenberg also shared. "So, my life feels pretty separate. My wife is a teacher. My kid doesn't really even watch movies. So, I'm not like knee-deep in the world of constantly trying to assess my own status in an industry."

After appearing in such projects as Buffy the Vampire Slayer and 2000's Bring It On, Dushku revealed in September 2024 that she had become certified in psychedelic-assisted therapy and is furthering her studies as a mental health professional.

"I had the means to shift directions and choose a course in my life that focused on healing myself so that I could help heal others," she told Boston Magazine. "I would be remiss if I didn’t now share the transformation and the peace and the passion that I have. This is just absolutely so clearly my real calling, my real purpose."

The Flintstones star revealed that she moved to Ireland in January 2025 with her youngest child Clay and was in the process of getting her Irish citizenship as her grandparents are from the European country. But while Rosie cited recent political developments as her reason for leaving, she didn’t rule out an eventual return home.

"I miss my other kids," she said in a video on TikTok. "I miss my friends. I miss many things about life there at home and I'm trying to find a home here in in this beautiful country. And when it is safe for all citizens to have equal rights there in America, that's when we will consider coming back."

The Ant-Man and the Wasp star announced she's taking an indefinite hiatus from acting after 20 years in the industry.

"I am so filled with joy and contentment today as I live out my vision," Lilly wrote on Instagram in June 2024. "I feel so grateful for my blessings. Stepping away from what seems like the obvious choice (wealth and fame) can feel scary at times, but stepping into your dharma replaces the fear with fulfillment."

But she isn't necessarily shutting the door, either, adding, "I might return to Hollywood one day, but, for now, this is where I belong."

The Vampire Diaries alum hasn't sunk his teeth into a new role since Netflix's 2019 series V-Wars. Instead, he has dug a little deeper into a passion project, namely his mission to combat climate change by improving the world's soil.

"I stepped away from acting a little over four years ago to raise my kids, build my companies and get these films launched," Somerhalder, who shares two children with wife Nikki Reed, told E! News in November 2023 of launching the 2020 documentary Kiss the Ground and its follow up Common Ground, each detailing the need for regenerative farming.

When he looks years down the road, the actor continued, "I will be a rancher and building legacy brands, whether it's my bourbon or my health and wellness company, and the regenerative agriculture and healthy soil management practices that I live by and our family lives by. That's where my life was going. So when people say 'Why do you care?' That's why I care. Because that's who I am, that's what I'm going to become."

On a February 2021 episode of her podcast Empty Inside, the iCarly alum told guest Anna Faris that she decided to stop acting a few years back and is now focused on opportunities in writing and directing, in addition to hosting the podcast.

"My experience with acting is, I'm so ashamed of the parts I've done in the past," revealed McCurdy, who detailed her experience in her 2022 memoir I'm Glad My Mom Died. "I resent my career in a lot of ways. I feel so unfulfilled by the roles that I played and felt like it was the most cheesy, embarrassing. I did the shows that I was on from like 13 to 21, and by 15, I was already embarrassed. My friends at 15, they're not like, 'Oh, cool, you're on this Nickelodeon show.' It was embarrassing."

Though she hasn't totally written off a second act. "I do feel like only through writing the book have I gotten to a place where I think there might be a way of exploring acting that doesn't carry that baggage that I carried with me for so long," she told E! News in October 2022. "Maybe if I write something for myself. I think that'd really be maybe one of the only ways I could kind of try exploring it again."

This felt like something of a no-brainer. If we had a shot to marry Prince Harry, dedicate our life to the philanthropic causes that matter most to us and gain access to the Queen's impressive collection of tiaras, bidding ta-ta to Tinseltown would feel like an okay sacrifice.

Following the path Grace Kelly took from Hollywood to the Palace of Monaco, Meghan left behind her home in Toronto—and her breakout role on Suits—for a life in The Firm. Though, now that she and Harry have shed their senior roles and live in Montecito, Calif., she's edging back into the business thanks to business moves like their multi-year production deal with Netflix. The Duchess of Sussex released her 2022 docuseries Harry & Meghan as well as her 2025 lifestyle show With Love, Meghan on the streaming service. She's also launched podcasts and her brand As Ever.

Having made upwards of 40 movies since her debut in 1994's The Mask, the actress was long overdue for a break when filming wrapped on 2014's Annie.

"I just decided that I wanted different things out of my life," she explained to pal Gwyneth Paltrow of her ultimate act of self-care. "I had gone so hard for so long, working, making films and it's such a grind. When you're making a movie—it's a perfect excuse—they own you. You're there for 12 hours a day for months on end and you have no time for anything else."

And there was plenty more she'd like to explore, from writing (she followed up her 2013 New York Times best-seller The Body Book with 2016's The Longevity Book) to starting a family with husband Benji Madden. But while Cameron confessed to InStyle in 2019, "I don't miss performing. Right now I'm looking at the landscape of wellness and all that," apparently she could be swayed.

"We just begged and pleased on my knees, like, 'Just give the people one more again,'" Jamie Foxx told E! News of getting Diaz to sign on for the 2025 Netflix film Back in Action. "We love her, we've been waiting on her and this is just gonna be fantastic."

The actor insisted there'd be no encore after he finished his five-year run on Empire. When Extra asked Howard about his future ahead of the musical drama series' sixth and final season in 2019, he responded, "Oh, I'm done with acting. I'm done pretending."

And though he returned to set for a handful of projects, the Oscar nominee again announced his plans to quit acting while promoting his Peacock series The Best Man: The Final Chapters in 2022. "I've gotten to the point where now I've given the very best that I have as an actor," he told ET. "Now I'm enjoying watching other new talent come around, and I don't want to do an impersonation of myself."

Despite these comments, though, Howard has since appeared in a few more shows and movies, including the TV series Fight Night: The Million Dollar Heist and Netflix film Shirley, with multiple projects lined up in the future.

Once his time as King Joffrey came to a sudden, purple-faced end in 2014, the then-21-year-old told EW he was getting out of the game. "I've been acting since age 8," the Game of Thrones star explained of his decision. "I just stopped enjoying it as much as I used to."

No longer a child star, a bit of the magic had worn off. "Now there's the prospect of doing it for a living, whereas up until now it was always something I did for recreation with my friends, or in the summer for some fun," Gleeson continued. "I enjoyed it. When you make a living from something, it changes your relationship with it. It's not like I hate it, it's just not what I want to do."

But after a six-year break, he was ready to resume his reign, joining the cast of BBC's series Out of Her Mind in 2020. Since then, Jack has also appeared in movies like Rebecca's Boyfriend and In the Land of Saints and Sinners as well as TV shows like Safe Harbor and The Famous Five.

When Fast Times at Ridgemont High's dream girl (Jennifer Aniston took on her part in September 2020's virtual table read) wed fellow actor Kevin Kline in 1989, they "agreed to alternate so that we're never working at the same time," he told Playboy of their plan to care for son Owen and daughter Greta (a singer who now goes by the stage name Frankie Cosmos).

However, he continued, "whenever it's been her slot to work, Cates has chosen to stay with the children." Though she made a cameo in pal Jennifer Jason Leigh's 2001 indie The Anniversary Party, Phoebe devotes most of her time to operating her New York City boutique Blue Tree.

At the height of his Ghostbusters and Honey, I... fame, the '80s star stepped away from filmmaking not long after his wife passed away from breast cancer in 1991 to focus on raising his kids Rachel and Mitchell.

Though Moranis hasn't had a live-action movie role since 1997, even passing on a cameo in Paul Feig's 2016 Ghostbusters remake, he's remained a treasured cultural icon, as evidenced by the outrage over reports that he'd been assaulted while walking in New York City in 2020.Thankfully there's good news for fans: He'll make his triumphant return alongside Josh Gad in the forthcoming Disney reboot Shrunk.

Once she wed fashion designer Adam Kimmel in 2010, the Never Been Kissed standout hinted that she was maybe kinda done with movies. "Ninety percent of acting roles involve so much sexual stuff with other people, and I don't want to do that," she explained to Vogue. "It's such a strange fire to play with, and our relationship is surely strong enough to handle it, but if you're going to walk through fire, there has to be something incredible on the other side."

Her decision was solidified after son Martin joined older sister Louisanna in 2014. "I don't do movie stuff anymore. I am totally an outsider! I … am just a mom and an outsider," she noted to Us Weekly at a 2016 event, explaining that she helps Kimmel with his business and paints on the side. "I am just focused on my kids. I think that's mainly why I stopped."

She'd done Ally McBeal. And Nip/Tuck. Then Arrested Development and finally Scandal when the Aussie realized that maybe she was ready to turn the dial.

"I was approaching 45 and I just kind of…was wondering is there something that I could tackle now that I've never done before that would be really challenging and different," she explained on wife Ellen DeGeneres' eponymous talk show in 2018. "I kind of knew what acting would look like for me for the next 10, 20 years, so I decided to quit and start a business."

Her consumer-art company, General Public, already a work in progress, she had just one piece to finish.

"I called Mitch Hurwitz, who's the creator of Arrested Development and I said, 'If there is a season 5, I won't be doing it because I quit acting. And he seemed really understanding and he totally got it. We had a great conversation, and then he wrote me into five episodes."

To be fair, once you've won three Academy Awards, what's left to accomplish? Shortly after receiving his sixth Oscar nod for his final film, 2017's Phantom Thread, the thespian had his rep issue a statement informing fans that he "will no longer be working as an actor. He is immensely grateful to all of his collaborators and audiences over the many years. This is a private decision and neither he nor his representatives will make any further comment on this subject."

But just when Day-Lewis thought he was out, his son pulled him back in. In October 2024, production company Focus Features announced the Oscar winner would star in 2025's Anemone, the film he wrote alongside son Ronan Day-Lewis.

The Good Luck Charlie alum took a step back from the spotlight in 2018 when she began pursuing a master's degree from MIT, later earning a PhD from the institution. She also enrolled in Harvard Law School.

And as if that weren't enough, Mendler launched her own startup Northwood Space, which aims to build ground satellite stations to help send and receive data from space, becoming CEO of the brand in February 2023.

#906. ‘Pregnancy does not mean game over’: meet the footballers challenging the myths | Moving the Goalposts

Claire Emslie and Emma Kelly are among those taking advantage of new research and guidelines for pregnant players

Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant.

Emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC, documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset. Rather than marking the end of a career (notably, Millie Bright announced her pregnancy in September, months after having retired), pregnancy can mark both a continuation and a renewal.

“I think it’s becoming more common. You’re seeing it more often, especially in America,” says 32-year-old Emslie, who trained at high intensity throughout her pregnancy, with a three-person team looking after her. She gave birth to her son, Jamie, in December 2025 and returned to competitive action by May 2026; scoring her first goal since coming back for Scotland in October, and her first club goal this month. “It’s amazing what the body can do. I debunked a lot of myths that I’d heard about being pregnant.”

For many years, says the physiotherapist and Women’s Football Hub founder Carolyn Kent, there was huge caution around high-impact sports and pregnancy. The fear was that overexertion and physical contact – a heart rate going too high, a bad fall, a mistimed kick to the abdomen – could cause miscarriage. But slowly this is changing. In July Fifa launched its Stay in Play guidelines and research, which offer a groundbreaking framework for decision-making around football participation during pregnancy.

“I was always told that once you hit that first trimester, 12 weeks, all contact stops. But actually they’re now saying, no, we need to be a little bit more nuanced than that,” says Kent. The research suggests that while that timeframe should still be considered the loose recommended cut-off point for full-contact football (due to the uterus growing over the pubic bone and offering less protection for the growing foetus in the second trimester), low-contact and modified training can continue in the absence of any medical reason for it not to.

“Pregnancy does not mean game over,” adds Kent. “It does not mean that ‘OK, I’ve got to automatically stop’. That again feeds into this narrative that females are fragile. Your body’s amazing.”

Up to 2021, only 6% of sports science research was done on women, which means gaps are still being filled in. But as the women’s game continues to grow, this is happening at speed, says Sinéad Dufour, a pelvic health physiotherapist and academic who was one of the researchers who developed the Stay in Play guidelines. She gives Fifa credit for recognising the development of the women’s game – its popularity and intensity has soared in the past 10 years with more than six million women and girls playing football in England alone.

“More and more players are now staying through until they’re having families … And they put all this money into research,” she says. They have identified “clear cut” physical and mental health benefits for women to keep up with football, including a lower injury risk postpartum.

“There’s always been a notion that women just aren’t strong and robust the way we actually are, and now the science is proving otherwise,” Dufour says. “I do think some of it relates to the foetus. That’s going to supersede what’s actually good for the woman, right?”

Some of the main considerations players should have, whether professional or amateur, as to whether they should keep playing and training throughout pregnancy, relate to pain, pelvic floor dysfunction, and motor control and movement, she adds. But the decision whether or not to continue playing during pregnancy is ultimately personal.

When Emma Kelly, who plays for Newcastle, unexpectedly became pregnant earlier this year at the age of 29, she was anxious. She had never played with a pregnant teammate before and she had been out for much of the season due to injury. How isolating would the experience be? Was it going to jeopardise her career? “I was questioning whether this is the right time,” she says. “It’s not that I’m ungrateful but it’s just finding it hard being out of the team again and not being able to play the sport that I love.”

Though she continued to train, she and her partner decided she would stop contact football immediately, prior to 12 weeks, as “football is so unpredictable”, she says. As she didn’t want to announce her pregnancy until she was into the second trimester, in the interim she told her teammates that she was unwell. Like Emslie she has been documenting her training with the encouragement of her club and feels as if she is noticing more and more athletes doing the same. “I want to continue as long as my body allows me to,” she says. Her club has been “extremely supportive” with specialised training, physio and equipment.

But for all the newfound positivity around pre-and postpartum for footballers, Emslie says candidly, there are some hard truths that players have to face: namely that pregnancy is a sacrifice. The pitch is their stage and no player wants to be relegated to the role of understudy, relearning how to bend their body to their will. “If I wasn’t worried about [fertility], I wouldn’t have gotten pregnant till I was retired,” she says. “I could have had a full football career.”

The other is that football is a business. “You’re used as a player,” she says bluntly. “As soon as you turn a certain age, or if you’ve got a kid, they look at you different … As a player, you’re wanted until you’re not.” Though she made it clear she wasn’t talking about her own club, which was very supportive of her pregnancy and return, at the time of interview she was two months away from her contract ending with Angel City but had no news of a new deal being offered.

Even so, Dufour says, the body works hard during pregnancy; aerobic capacity is pushed. “The biggest stress test you’re ever going to go through is pregnancy,” she says. Her data shows that some women will achieve personal bests on their return. In short pregnancy could be a secret superpower. In an industry as capitalistic, brutal and data-driven as football, that’s an important fact.

#905. Odegaard backing Norway to avenge Wales defeat

Arsenal's Premier League-winning captain Martin Odegaard also wears the armband for Norway

Martin Odegaard admits snow disruption has affected Norway's preparations for Saturday's Nations League meeting with Wales â but the Arsenal captain is backing his team to avenge their defeat in Cardiff last month.

Wales beat the World Cup quarter-finalists 2-1 for their only win of the campaign so far, with Norway head coach Stale Solbakken describing the first-half performance as their worst for two years.

Norway had to train indoors on Thursday because the Ullevaal Stadion pitch, which was criticised earlier this year before being repaired in the summer, was covered in snow.

That snow was cleared on Friday, allowing Norway to resume training in Oslo as they look to climb off the bottom of Group A4.

How do you stop Haaland? Wales show how it's done

Wales' James warns of Norwegian revenge in Oslo

They have three points out of six from four games, the same tally as Wales, but are below Craig Bellamy's side in third because of their head-to-head record.

"Obviously we wanted to train yesterday, so it's not ideal but you have to adapt to the situation, and I think it's not the end of the world," Odegaard said.

On the defeat in Wales, the Arsenal midfielder added: "Our level was not where it should be. I think it's probably the only game for a long time where we haven't been playing to our standards.

"Wales is a good team, a competitive team, lots of good players in big leagues and a physical team as well, and we were prepared for that.

"But I think on the day we were just not showing up to our standards and that's something we want to show tomorrow [Saturday], and we can do a lot better. We want to show a different version tomorrow."

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC Two Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live Sports Extra, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

Having been unbeaten in 2025 before impressing with their run to the last eight at this summer's World Cup, Norway have lost their past three matches , with 2-1 defeats against Portugal either side of their loss by the same score in Cardiff.

Norway and Wales still have a chance of finishing second behind Portugal, but they are also battling each other to avoid potential relegation from the Nations League's top tier.

"It's like a boxing game, going head-to-head, fist-to-fist," said Solbakken.

"I think Wales has always been a very attacking team under Bellamy. They've had great progress with the ball.

"I think it suits the team with the offensive players they have, the speed on the wings and Harry Wilson back. And [Lewis] Koumas getting more minutes for Liverpool, so I think that suits them.

"I'm not surprised that they will go all in but it's our home game so obviously I think they will also have their struggles with us. Let's see."

Wales head coach Bellamy and winger Daniel James, who scored their first goal in Cardiff last month, have said they are mindful of Norway's desire to exact revenge.

Asked if that was an incentive for his side, Solbakken said: "I think both teams need to win the game, so you can call it revenge or whatever.

"I think we were very passive in the first half against Wales. We had no intensity in our play. We were decent with the ball, but we were crap without the ball.

"Overall, they deserved to lead by half-time and then there was our red card one minute into the second half.

"I think the first half was our worst performance in two years, we have to be honest about that.

"It's two aims for us now in this football year. That is to at least be going for the third place first, and that we can do tomorrow. It's a crucial game."

#903. Some EFL clubs beggar belief - Walsall's Pomlett

Boyhood Walsall fan Leigh Pomlett first joined the Saddlers board in 2010

Walsall co-chairman Leigh Pomlett has given a powerful response to the independent State of the Game report by suggesting some clubs "beggar belief" in the way they operate.

The revelation of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) in its first report that 94% of clubs made losses in the 2025-26 season suggested the majority of clubs were living "on the edge of financial disaster".

Pomlett told BBC Radio WM at a Walsall fans' forum at Bescot Stadium just how serious football's financial problems are. And, although he stressed that the Saddlers are better run than most, the League Two promotion contenders will still have to make significant cuts in spending to qualify for an IFR operating licence in future.

"The State of the Game report came out a couple of weeks ago," he said. "A report that has come out from the independent regulator. It is a huge report and I have, for my sins, read all 260 pages of it.

"It goes into huge detail and, for the first time ever, is about the state of English football, right from the Premier League to the National League.

"Football is in a shocking state. Some clubs would still lose money even if they paid their players nothing. That is a fact. Some clubs will have to radically change what they do."

Majority of clubs on edge of 'financial disaster' - regulator

"Compared to some clubs, we at Walsall are in a very good state of health but it's still tough - just a lot less tough than it will be for some other clubs in the EFL who just beggar belief.

"We are at times accused of lack of ambition for not being able to buy this or that player, but the priority is still to make the club sustainable."

In a week when fellow Midlands-based League Two club Shrewsbury Town were taken over by new American owners, Pomlett warns that the scope for any club looking to speculate to accumulate will have to be drastically toned down if the regulator deduces they are spending money they have not got.

"The losses from the top to the bottom are massive," said Pomlett.

"Clubs who are losing an absolute fortune every week will not be allowed to continue like that.

"Thirty-three clubs do not have enough cash to survive a month. That's incredible.

"The losses being made in League One, League Two and the National League are enormous, but some of the Premier League and Championship losses are mind-boggling.

"The regulator is not going to let us carry on like that.

"We're on the brink of the biggest change in the football industry that we've seen since the Premier League was first formed."

After the BBC Radio WM Football Phone-In slot, a fuller recording of the Fans Forum will be posted on Sounds at 19:00 GMT.

#902. Danny Kelly, football broadcaster and renowned editor, dies aged 69

Danny Baker pays tribute to the ‘funniest man I knew’

Kelly was former editor of the NME and Q magazines

The journalist and broadcaster Danny Kelly, who helped define coverage of music and football in the UK for a generation, has died at the age of 69.

Kelly edited the NME and Q magazine, and launched the Football 365 website before going on to be a presenter and pundit on the BBC and TalkSport. He had been receiving treatment for oesophageal cancer.

Tributes were led by Kelly’s longstanding broadcast partner Danny Baker. “My great friend, supreme broadcaster and funniest man I ever knew, Danny Kelly, died yesterday afternoon,” Baker wrote on social media, the pair having worked together on any number of radio, TV shows and podcasts. “I cannot believe I will never hear his voice again.”

Tottenham Hotspur paid emotional tribute to Kelly, a lifelong Spurs fan. A statement said: “The entire Tottenham family mourns the loss of one of our own, broadcasting legend Danny Kelly. Our thoughts and love are with his family and friends at this incredibly sad time.”

TalkSport, for which Kelly worked as a presenter for nearly two decades, said it was “heartbroken” by the news. “A cherished part of TalkSport for so many years, Danny brought extraordinary wit, warmth and knowledge to our airwaves,” the station said. “His passion for football, music and life was infectious, and his kindness touched everyone around him.”

Another broadcaster, the former Sky Sports host Richard Keys, said Kelly “was all of the things – and more – being said about him – ‘warm, witty and knowledgable’”.

Kelly was born in north London in 1956 and first made his name writing about music. He began contributing to the NME in his 20s and went on to edit the agenda-setting weekly newspaper at the end of the 1980s. From there he took charge of the top-selling music monthly Q magazine, where he was named British magazine editor of the year.

Manic Street Preachers paid tribute to “a brilliant broadcaster-writer-ideas factory. Danny was editor of the NME when we first started getting press, a wonderful man, his musical knowledge was vast and deep, his radio voice has been part of our lives for so long … We will all miss him.”

In the second half of the 1990s, Kelly threw himself into the nascent world of digital media and launched Football365, which became one of the leading online voices on the sport. In the noughties, he spotted another development – podcasts – and launched the Game, a weekly football podcast, for the Times.

Over the past 15 years Kelly became best known as a radio presenter and podcast host, including presenting the Tottenham-focused show View from The Lane. Paying tribute to “our host, our leader” on its X account, the View from the Lane said: “We all loved him as much as he loved Spurs.”
